Kageaki"Our main targets are the teams that did not compete today. Most should be in their paddock garages, preparing their machines for tomorrow's main qualifying."
Kageaki"Some may take practice flights on the course. Those are Muramasa's responsibility. We shall pass ourselves off as people connected with racing, enter the garages and collect information from the teams."
Kageaki"Security should be lighter than during the race. So long as nobody makes himself conspicuously suspicious, there should be no difficulty. If you do arouse suspicion, withdraw promptly. Kindly do not force the matter."
Kanae"Question!"
Kageaki"Yes, Captain."
Kanae"In which direction shall we take the questioning? 'Excuse me, might you know anything about Silver Star?' Along those lines?"
Ichijou"That's not a direction, that's straight into it! At least put one bend in the question!"
Kageaki"Once they suspect us, the operation is finished. Harmless conversation first. Quite often, something unexpected comes out of ordinary chatting itself."
Kageaki"If a direction must be specified... look for someone starved for power."
Kanae"Meaning?"
Kageaki"It appears to be a tendency among the hosts Silver Star selects."

She holds out the object she has had in her hands all this time. A piece of metal—a drive-wing bearing, perhaps.

...Of course. Her precious machine for tomorrow's main qualifying, that is what she has been servicing.

Servicing a sword-armor is a mechanic's job. But not every little task requires specialist craftsmanship. An amateur can help with the simple work. No law says a racer must not.

A matter of temperament, whether one does. Many refuse to do any of it, call that a rider's pride. She, apparently, is one who does.

en.html:
A fine-featured face turns my way. At first it stirs no memory. Too different. Suguru Oji, once Yamato's greatest rider, never wore glasses. Nor did he have this gentle expression.

I look almost to the point of rudeness, then reconsider. Remove the glasses, turn back the years: yes, that rider is here. And the expression—I have read about that in magazines. In private, they said, he was so mild as to seem another man.

Almost frail, this smile. No trace in it of the starving wolf that used to tear into an opponent's defenses. Even so, there is no mistake. Suguru Oji.

He nods ambiguously. In that moment, the feelings passing across his face are far too complicated to untangle.

—Yes. The war. It took his dream of the world away.

The very year Suguru Oji conquered the domestic field and stood ready to go to Europe, the Great War broke out.

...By the time it ended six years ago, his physical prime was long past. No failure of effort, no lack of talent: somewhere entirely outside all that, his dream had been crushed. His bitterness can only be imagined.
